sections.learningObjectives:
- Describe patient financial responsibility and identify which charges become the patient's obligation after payer processing.
- Explain how patient responsibility varies by payer and plan, including networks, cost sharing, and coverage rules.
- Calculate patient responsibility from allowed amounts, deductibles, coinsurance, and coordination of benefits.
- Communicate balances and financial responsibility to patients respectfully, privately, and within the assistant's scope of practice.
sections.eli10:
### Question 1

Think of a restaurant bill where your friend (the insurance) pays part and a coupon lowers the total; the leftover you pay is your responsibility.

### Question 2

An EOB is like a receipt that shows the insurance paid this much and you still owe that much, but it is not the actual bill.

### Question 3

The premium is like a monthly gym membership fee; the copay, deductible, and coinsurance are extra costs when you actually use a service.

### Question 4

A copay is a flat entrance fee, like paying the same small set price every time you ride the bus no matter how far you go.

### Question 5

The deductible is like the first portion of a long hike you must walk alone before your friend starts helping carry the load.

### Question 6

Coinsurance is like splitting a pizza by percentage, you and the insurance each pay your slice of the cost.

### Question 7

The write-off is like a store discount the seller agrees to absorb; the customer never pays the discounted-away part.

### Question 8

A self-pay patient is like someone buying an item with cash because they have no gift card or coupon to help pay.

### Question 9

Your leftover amount is like your piggy bank total minus what others already paid in and minus any discounts.

### Question 10

A financial policy is like the rules card at a game table, it tells everyone the rules for paying before the game starts.

### Question 11

Checking benefits is like checking your gift card balance before you shop so you know how much you will need to add yourself.

### Question 12

Medicare is like a national safety net for older adults and some people with disabilities to help pay for care.

### Question 13

Medicaid is like a shared piggy bank from the state and the nation that helps people with lower incomes get care.

### Question 14

Two students buying the same lunch can pay different amounts if one has a lunch card with different rules than the other.

### Question 15

An in-network provider is like a shop that agreed to special lower prices with your membership card.

### Question 16

Some check-ups are like free samples the insurance gives you so you stay healthy without paying extra.

### Question 17

The allowed amount is like the sticker price the store and the coupon company actually agree on.

### Question 18

The EOB is the note from the insurance explaining the math, and the statement is the actual bill asking you to pay.

### Question 19

A statement is like the itemized receipt and bill you get that shows each charge and what you still owe.

### Question 20

When two grown-ups both offer to help pay, coordination of benefits decides who goes first and who covers the leftovers.

### Question 21

Talking about money is private, like a secret; you should discuss it quietly in a private room, not where everyone can hear.

### Question 22

Be kind when someone cannot pay, like helping a friend find a way to pay later instead of making them feel bad.

### Question 23

You should not erase a fee on your own; instead, follow the office rule book and ask a manager.

### Question 24

The copay is like a set ticket price you collect when the patient arrives, not something to skip or let the patient choose.

### Question 25

Until the deductible piggy bank is full, the patient pays the visit cost and it gets dropped into that piggy bank.

### Question 26

If the cost is $100 and you pay 20 cents of every dollar, you pay $20 and the insurance pays the rest.

### Question 27

When the safety jar is completely full, the insurance pays for everything covered, so your share is zero.

### Question 28

If a coupon does not cover an item, you pay the whole price for that item yourself.

### Question 29

Balance billing is like a store asking you to pay the extra between the sale price and the original price, which is usually not allowed for in-network shops.

### Question 30

An HMO is like a team you must stay within and get permission to visit certain players, while a PPO gives you more freedom to roam.

### Question 31

A high-deductible plan is like buying a cheaper membership but paying more out of your own pocket before the membership starts helping.

### Question 32

For most Medicare doctor visits, the insurance pays about 80 cents of each dollar and the patient pays about 20 cents.

### Question 33

Medicaid is like a different rule book in each state, so you must check the patient's specific page before knowing what they owe.

### Question 34

When someone has both programs, Medicare pays first like the main helper, and Medicaid steps in to cover the leftover bits.

### Question 35

When two notes about money do not match, be a detective and find the missing piece before deciding what is owed.

### Question 36

Checking ahead is like reading the menu prices before ordering so there are no surprises when the bill arrives.

### Question 37

Getting permission first is like asking a parent before a big purchase; without permission, you may have to pay for it yourself.

### Question 38

A PPO is like a card that works a little at other stores, while an HMO mostly works only at its own store except in an emergency.

### Question 39

Every plan is like a different recipe; you cannot assume two plans have the same ingredients.

### Question 40

The store asked $300, the coupon lowered it to $220, insurance paid 80 percent, and you pay the remaining 20 percent, which is $44.

### Question 41

Different stores negotiate different sale prices with the supplier, so the same item can cost different amounts at different stores.

### Question 42

The EOB is the explainer note from insurance, and the statement is the bill from the doctor's office; you pay the bill, not the note.

### Question 43

You can give a best-guess price, like estimating how much groceries will cost, while reminding them the register total may be a little different.

### Question 44

When someone questions a bill, first listen carefully, then look at the papers together to explain, and ask a grown-up for help if it is still confusing.

### Question 45

If a friend is short on money, be kind, share what help is available, and ask a manager who can arrange a payment plan.

### Question 46

A payment plan is like an agreement to pay in installments; the person in charge of money sets it up and writes it down.

### Question 47

Some stores have special discount programs and some do not, so you check the store's rules before telling a customer they qualify.

### Question 48

If someone is standing too close while you talk about money, move to a quiet corner so only the right person hears.

### Question 49

Kind words about money sound like offering to look at the bill together instead of scolding someone.

### Question 50

When someone is upset, stay calm, let them talk, say you understand, and offer to look at the problem together.

### Question 51

Some questions, like tax rules, need a specialist; you say so kindly and point the person to the right expert.

### Question 52

Write down the plan like keeping a homework planner so everyone remembers what was agreed.

### Question 53

Teach-back is like asking a friend to explain the game rules back to you so you know they really got it.

### Question 54

When someone speaks another language, bring in a professional translator so the money talk is clear and private, not a family member.

### Question 55

An estimate is like a weather forecast; it is a good guess, but the real result may be a little different.

### Question 56

When someone owes money from before, quietly and kindly mention it in private and follow the office rules for collecting.

### Question 57

When two insurance plans help, the first pays first, and you send its receipt to the second so it can chip in for the rest.

### Question 58

Deciding who pays first follows a rule book, not a guess or a favorite, so you look up the correct order.

### Question 59

Accepting assignment is like agreeing to the store's set price and only asking the customer for their small share.

### Question 60

Some doctors who are not in the full agreement may add a small, capped extra charge, but there is a limit on how much extra they can ask.

### Question 61

Different recipe books allow different dishes, so what one plan covers another plan might not.

### Question 62

Once the deductible hurdle is cleared, the patient pays their percentage slice, which is 30 cents of each dollar here.

### Question 63

Wait for the insurance to finish its math before telling the patient their final amount, so you do not ask for too much.

### Question 64

After insurance pays its part, the leftover is usually your deductible, your percentage share, or something the plan does not cover.

### Question 65

Writing down the rules for paying ahead of time is like posting park rules at the gate so everyone knows what to expect.

### Question 66

When you cannot solve a money question yourself, hand it to the person in charge who can sort it out.

### Question 67

To find your leftover amount, take the price, subtract what both helpers paid, and subtract the discount, and whatever remains is yours to pay.

### Question 68

The safety net only catches things the plan covers; if an item is not covered, you pay for that item yourself even if the net is full.

### Question 69

Two classmates can pay different amounts for the same field trip if one has a discount card with different rules than the other.

### Question 70

If your share was $60 and the second helper paid $40 of it, you are left with $20 to pay.

### Question 71

Original Medicare is the main program, while Medicare Advantage is like a private-team version with its own rule book.

### Question 72

Medigap is like a second smaller piggy bank that helps pay the leftover coins that original Medicare leaves behind.

### Question 73

You cannot just erase a fee to be nice; doing it often breaks the rules, so it needs special permission.

### Question 74

If someone shares a money worry, take the talk to a private spot so no one else can hear their business.

### Question 75

You can give your best guess and remind them it might change a little, but you should never promise an exact number you cannot know yet.

### Question 76

Before asking the patient to pay for a denied item, check whether the paperwork can be fixed so the insurance pays instead.

### Question 77

One case is like an item the store never sells, and the other is like the store saying you did not need it, which you can argue with proof.

### Question 78

An ABN is like a heads-up note saying the insurance might not pay, so the patient can agree to pay if it does not.

### Question 79

On January 1, the savings jar is emptied and must be filled up again before the helper starts paying.

### Question 80

If a shop joined your membership program, it promised not to charge you the extra over the agreed price.

### Question 81

If a discount was missed in the math, fix the account and note the fix so the customer is charged the right amount.

### Question 82

Medicaid waits at the very back of the line and only pays the little bit left after everyone else has chipped in.

### Question 83

You cannot change a bill on your own; say so kindly and pass the request to the person who is allowed to review it.

### Question 84

Before paying cash for something, you get a written guess of the cost so you know what to expect, even if the final number shifts a little.
